title: Conceptual divergence analysis: LLM-assisted mapping of a researcher’s conceptual vocabulary against their curated literature
abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM)-based research tools often overlook a researcher-specific problem in manuscript writing: where does my use of a key theoretical term stand relative to the literature I want to address? We introduce Conceptual Divergence Analysis (CDA), an LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation pipeline to compare theoretical term usage in a researcher’s manuscripts with usage in a researcher-curated literature corpus. We propose reflective calibration as the individual-level scientometric function this workflow performs. We demonstrate CDA on two research programs, encompassing corpora of roughly 3,200 and 2,800 papers and four theoretical terms. The analyses reveal researcher-specific divergences consequential for theoretical positioning. In one case, the researcher draws a distinction the literature leaves underarticulated. In another case, CDA reveals how a term carries different meanings across disciplinary traditions, helping the researcher anticipate how different scholarly audiences may interpret its use. Register assignments are anchored to pre-computed clusters. An optional researcher-led validation step records the researcher’s judgment before revealing the model’s interpretation, making agreement or disagreement explicit. We release the complete pipeline as an open-source resource with a no-installation hosted demonstration on a public toy corpus, extending an individual-level tradition in scientometrics from citation structure to conceptual vocabulary.

title: Financial Constraints, Wages, and Macroeconomic Implications
authors: HAMZEH ARABZADEH; ALMUT BALLEER; BRITTA GEHRKE
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how firm‐level financial constraints affect individual wages and aggregate labor market dynamics during financial recessions. We derive testable predictions from competing theoretical mechanisms and assess them empirically using German administrative worker data matched to firm balance sheets. Embedding these microlevel estimates in a macroeconomic model with labor and financial frictions, we demonstrate how small ceteris paribus effects align with large aggregate dynamics. Tighter financial conditions amplify wage and unemployment volatility, weakening the tight link between wage rigidity and the volatility of unemployment discussed in the literature. Financial constraints reduce the effectiveness of hiring subsidies during recessions.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
authors: Lu Fang; Zhe Yuan; Kaifu Zhang; Dante Donati; Miklos Sarvary
affiliations: School of Management, Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics, Hangzhou 310018 China; and Laboratory for Human-AI Collaboration and Digital Intelligence Innovation, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058 China; Center for Research of Private Economy, School of Economics, Future Regional Development Laboratory, and Academy of Financial Research, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058 China; Individual Researcher; Columbia Business School, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
abstract: We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Over 2023–2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The gains operate primarily through higher conversion rates rather than larger cart values, consistent with GenAI improving the shopping experience by reducing search, information, communication, and personalization frictions. Importantly, these effects are not associated with worse postpurchase outcomes as product return rates and customer ratings do not deteriorate. Finally, we document substantial demand-side heterogeneity, with larger gains for less experienced consumers. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on how GenAI shapes sales productivity in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential. title: Trust Violations in Research Universities
affiliations: William G. Howell is Dean of the School of Government and Policy and Professor of Political Science, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland. His email address is .
abstract: By nearly twice as much as in any other institution that Gallup tracks, public trust in research universities has fallen over the past decade. The causes are not only external. This essay examines two violations of trust that originate within the academy: research that is driven by political advocacy, and a professoriate whose range of ideological viewpoints has narrowed, especially in the humanities and social sciences. The first subordinates the pursuit of truth to political aims; the second erodes the diversity of perspectives that checks individual biases and lets research correct itself. Both break faith with the arguments originally advanced for tenure and academic freedom. Restoring trust demands a renewed commitment to disinterested inquiry and the cultivation of intellectual pluralism—objectives, both, that are best adopted voluntarily, without state censor or interference, and promptly.

title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
affiliations: Dean Karlan is the Frederic Esser Nemmers Distinguished Professor of Economics and Finance, Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois. He served as Chief Economist, US Agency for International Development (USAID) from November 2022 to February 2025 and is the founder of Innovations for Poverty Action. His email address is
abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly motivated diverge. Breaking down the “why” and the “how” can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones. The “why” asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods. The “how” asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem. Evidence is central to the “how”: Use it where it exists, produce it where it does not. In particular, approaches that improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge. Ultimately, the “how” is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.

title: The Role of Private Debt in the Financial Ecosystem
affiliations: Victoria Ivashina is Professor of Business Administration, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts, and Research Associate, National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her email address is
abstract: This paper provides an introduction to the modern private debt market and examines its rapid expansion following the 2007–2009 global financial crisis. Traditionally, economists distinguished between public debt markets and private debt in the form of bank lending. In contemporary markets, however, “private debt” refers to credit originated and held by nonbank financial intermediaries, including private credit funds and business development companies. The paper reviews the key drivers of the sector’s growth; analyzes the distinctive features of private lending arrangements and funding structures; and discusses the implications for traditional banking, financial intermediation, and financial stability. While the sector’s rapid growth and increasing complexity warrant careful monitoring, the paper argues that private debt represents an important and likely durable component of modern financial markets.

title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
authors: David J. Deming; Raffaella Sadun; Christopher Stanton
affiliations: David J. Deming is Professor of Economics and Public Policy, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Raffaella Sadun is Professors of Business Administration, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts.; Christopher Stanton is Professors of Business Administration, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts.
abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This, in turn, makes general skill firm specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

title: The Meritocratic Consensus and Stratification in Higher Education
affiliations: Zachary Bleemer is Assistant Professor of Economics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey.; Jesse Rothstein is Professor of Public Policy and Economics and David Gardner Chair of Higher Education, University of California at Berkeley, Berkeley, California.
abstract: American colleges and universities are highly stratified by pre-college academic achievement, family background, and institutional resources. We study the meritocratic consensus in American higher education: Colleges that high-testing students (who are generally also from high-income families) attend spend dramatically more on instruction than do those that enroll lower-testing students. Stratification by test scores has been largely stable since the 1960s, but the stratification of instructional resources has risen sharply since 1970 at both private and public institutions. Nonacademic admissions criteria like athletics, legacy, and affirmative action are second-order in determining the allocation of students to universities. Potential economic justifications for the positive association of instructional expenditures with student prior achievement—q-complementarity between achievement and resources, convex social returns to high human capital, and incentives to invest in learning prior to college—have little empirical support. Resource stratification across universities has not increased in the past decade, largely due to increased public funding of universities that enroll lower-testing students through financial aid programs like California's CalGrant, but stratification within institutions is now rising swiftly.

title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
authors: Susan Athey; Neil Gandal; Tyler Moore
affiliations: Susan Athey is Professor of Economics, Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, Stanford, California.; Neil Gandal is Emeritus Professor of Economics, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel, and Professor of Cyber Studies, The University of Tulsa, Tulsa, Oklahoma.; Tyler Moore is Professor of Cybersecurity, The University of Tulsa, Tulsa, Oklahoma.
abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four central economic lessons and uses case studies, new data, and policy discussion to develop and support them.

title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
authors: Gregor Matvos; Tomasz Piskorski; Amit Seru
affiliations: Gregor Matvos is Professor of Finance, Northwestern Kellogg School of Business, Evanston, Illinois; and Research Associates, National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Tomasz Piskorski is Professor of Finance and Real Estate, Columbia Business School, New York City, New York; and Research Associates, National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Amit Seru is Professor of Finance, Stanford Business School, as well as Senior Fellow, Hoover Institution, and Senior Fellow, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, all at Stanford, California; and Research Associates, National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.
abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not currently replicate balance-sheet structures associated with banking fragility. We conclude by discussing potential vulnerabilities related to liquidity provision, valuation contagion, and loss transmission through investor balance sheets.

title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
authors: Isaiah Andrews; Sarah Moon; Jesse M. Shapiro
affiliations: Isaiah Andrews is the Charles E. and Susan T. Harris Professor of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts. Andrews is also Research Associates at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Sarah Moon is a PhD candidate in economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Jesse M. Shapiro is the George Gund Professor of Economics and Business Administration, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts. Shapiro is also Research Associates at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.
abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
authors: E. Jason Baron; Shawn Kantor; Alexander Whalley
affiliations: Jason Baron is Assistant Professor of Economics, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina. Baron is a Faculty Research Fellow and Kantor is a Research Associate, National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts.; Shawn Kantor is the L. Charles Hilton Jr. Distinguished Professor of Economics, Florida State University, Tallahassee, Florida.; Alexander Whalley is Professor of Economics, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada.
abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.
